headline: God Divided Light From Darkness: The Grammar of Sacred Colour
lede: An 1845 engraving from a book printed in fewer than a hundred copies has found a new audience in the esoteric corners of social media. Its author, Baron Frédéric de Portal, argued that every ancient civilization shared a symbolic language written in colour — and that the moment God divided light from darkness was its generative first word. The image is not decoration; it is a thesis.
body:
The curator account @ArchetypeVision shares an engraved plate from a book most colour theorists have never encountered. *An Essay on Symbolic Colours* appeared in English in 1845 in a print run of roughly a hundred copies — a London edition of a French original, *Des couleurs symboliques dans l'Antiquité, le Moyen Âge et les Temps modernes*, published eight years earlier. Its author, Baron Frédéric de Portal (1804–1876), was no cloistered mystic: a diplomat who served in Dresden and Saint Petersburg before settling into a senior post at the Council of State in Paris, he was an erudite administrator who pursued comparative religion with the precision of a legal brief.

Portal's argument is synthetic and audacious. Every ancient civilization — Persian, Egyptian, Indian, Greek, Hebrew, Christian — shared, he claimed, a **symbolic language written in colour**, a common chromatic vocabulary encoding spiritual truths. The framework rests on a cosmological axiom: light and darkness are the two primordial principles from which every hue descends. White denotes divine wisdom in its pure state; black, the principle of negation; red, divine love; blue, the animating breath or *ruah*. Portal identified *Zoroastrianism* — the Persian religion centred on the cosmic opposition of Ahura Mazda, lord of light, against Angra Mainyu, lord of darkness — as the oldest surviving articulation of this grammar, more systematic than even the Hebrew tradition whose Genesis account furnished the illustration.

"And God Divided Light From Darkness" is not decoration; it is argument. The first act of creation narrated in Genesis 1:4 — the separation of light from darkness — is, within Portal's schema, the generative cosmological event from which all colour, all symbol, and all sacred meaning descends. The Zoroastrian reading sits alongside the biblical one rather than displacing it: both are evidence of the same primordial truth expressed in different cultural registers. For Portal's tiny readership of architects, antiquarians, and esoteric initiates, the engraving functioned as a visual thesis statement: the *dyad* at the origin of everything visible.

Despite its minuscule circulation, the book left a detectable trace. Éliphas Lévi, whose *Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie* (1854–1856) became the foundational text of modern Western *ceremonial magic*, drew on Portal's colour schema as he wove *Kabbalah*, *Hermeticism*, and *Neoplatonism* into a single occult system. Through Lévi the framework entered the bloodstream of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and, beyond it, the modern esoteric revival. The parallel with Goethe's *Theory of Colours* (1810) is striking: Goethe also built his phenomenology on the light/darkness polarity, arguing that yellow was light darkened and blue darkness lightened. Where Goethe's project was perceptual and aesthetic, Portal's was theological and historical; both arrived at the same dyad.

The book's resurrection — via Imagier Publishing's 2009 reprint, the first English-language edition in 164 years, and the circulation of its plates on accounts like @ArchetypeVision — is itself a small cultural fact. Images from this tradition resurface in cycles: they appealed to the Romantics, to the Victorian occult revival, to Theosophists and symbolist painters, and now to an algorithmically constituted audience for whom a Zoroastrian-inflected reading of Genesis is a few swipes from a meme. Whether this constitutes genuine influence or mere aestheticization is a question Portal's text, rigorous for its time, could not have anticipated.

concepts.definition: The practice of assigning fixed spiritual or cosmic meanings to specific colours across religious, ritual, and artistic traditions. Portal's book argues that this practice was not culturally contingent but reflected a universal grammar shared by every ancient civilization, traceable to the primordial opposition of light and darkness.

The ancient Persian religion founded by the prophet Zoroaster, centred on the radical opposition of Ahura Mazda (the wise lord of light and truth) and Angra Mainyu (the destructive spirit of darkness). Its strict dualism made it Portal's model for the primordial light/darkness opposition that he believed underlay all colour symbolism across civilizations.

Hebrew word meaning breath, wind, or spirit — used in the opening verses of Genesis to describe the spirit of God moving over the waters at creation. In Portal's symbolic register, blue is associated with this animating divine breath, functioning as colour-made-theology.

In philosophy, a fundamental pair of opposing principles — here, light and darkness — whose interaction generates a more complex order. Portal treats the light/dark dyad as the generative origin of the entire symbolic colour spectrum; Goethe, working independently, arrived at the same two-pole structure from a phenomenological direction.

A structured tradition of ritual magic in the Western esoteric lineage, systematized in the nineteenth century by Éliphas Lévi and later codified by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. It synthesizes Kabbalah, astrology, and elaborate symbolic correspondences — including colour scales — into graded initiatory practices.

The Jewish mystical tradition concerned with the hidden structure of divinity and its relationship to creation, often visualized through the Tree of Life (a diagram of ten divine attributes, or sefirot). Lévi and the Golden Dawn adapted Kabbalah into the framework of Western ceremonial magic, assigning specific colour correspondences to each divine attribute.

A philosophical and magical tradition deriving from texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, emphasizing correspondence between the macrocosm (the divine order of the universe) and the microcosm (the human soul). It underpins Western esotericism's interest in symbolic correspondences, including the idea that colour encodes cosmic truths.

A late-antique philosophical tradition, drawing on Plato, that posits the emanation of all reality from a transcendent divine One. Medieval Christian theology absorbed Neoplatonic ideas about divine light, feeding directly into the symbolic reading of colour in Gothic cathedral art and later esoteric systems.

concepts.term: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
concepts.definition: A British magical society founded in 1888, whose members included W. B. Yeats and Aleister Crowley, that synthesized Kabbalah, astrology, tarot, and ceremonial magic into a graded initiatory system. Its elaborate colour scales for the divine attributes — descended from the Lévi and Portal lineage — became canonical in modern Western esotericism.

books.title: An Essay on Symbolic Colours, in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and Modern Times
books.author: Frédéric Portal (trans. W. S. Inman)
books.summary: Originally published in French in 1837 as *Des couleurs symboliques*, and translated into English in 1845 in an edition of roughly a hundred copies. Portal argues that every ancient civilization shared a symbolic language of colour derived from the primordial opposition of light and darkness, which he traces from Zoroastrianism through Egyptian, Greek, Hebrew, and Christian traditions. The book influenced Éliphas Lévi and, through him, the modern esoteric revival. It was not reprinted in English until 2009.

books.title: Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie
books.author: Éliphas Lévi
books.summary: Published in two volumes in 1854–1856, this is the foundational text of modern Western ceremonial magic. Lévi synthesized Kabbalah, Hermeticism, astrology, and tarot — drawing in part on Portal's colour symbolism — into a coherent occult system that shaped the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, Theosophy, and all subsequent Western esoteric practice. Its influence on occult colour theory is direct and documented.

books.title: Theory of Colours (Zur Farbenlehre)
books.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
books.summary: Published in German in 1810, Goethe's colour theory challenged Newton's purely optical account by insisting on colour as a phenomenon of perception and relationship. Like Portal, Goethe built his framework on the polarity of light and darkness, arguing that all colours arise from their interaction. The book influenced painters, psychologists, and esotericists far beyond its scientific reception, and its convergence with Portal's theological project — both men centering on the same dyad — is striking.
